blocks.content: The International Date Line bends and zig-zags across the Pacific Ocean to ensure that land areas under a single administration share the same calendar day.

blocks.title: Key Takeaways
items: The International Date Line (IDL) is an imaginary line located roughly at the 180° meridian in the Pacific Ocean.
Crossing the IDL from West to East subtracts a calendar day (gaining 24 hours), whereas crossing from East to West advances a calendar day.
The line deviates from the true 180° meridian to prevent island groups and landmasses under the same administration from having different dates.
Key geographic bodies traversed by or near the IDL include the Bering Strait, Chukchi Sea, and the Bering Sea.

rows: Passes mainly through the Pacific Ocean
Straight line from North to South Pole
Boundary separating two consecutive calendar dates

items: Directional Rule: Crossing West to East = Gain a day; Crossing East to West = Lose a day.
Geography Check: The IDL passes through the Bering Strait, dividing Russian Siberia and American Alaska.
Line Geometry: Unlike the Prime Meridian (0°), the International Date Line is not a straight line from pole to pole.
